_about: Question bank for the US real estate salesperson licensing exam, NATIONAL portion only. Every US state exam splits into a national section (roughly 60 to 80 of the questions, identical everywhere) and a state section (state law, which differs). These cover the national section. Anything that varies by state is either avoided or explicitly flagged in the explanation.
_disclaimer: A study aid written from standard exam content outlines, not official prep material and not legal advice. Always confirm against your own state's approved course.

questions.q: A seller's agent learns the seller must move quickly because of a job transfer. A buyer asks why the seller is moving. What must the agent do?
choices: Tell the buyer, because agents must disclose all material facts
Keep it confidential, because it would weaken the seller's negotiating position
Tell the buyer only if the buyer asks twice
Disclose it to the buyer's agent but not the buyer
questions.why: Confidentiality is a fiduciary duty owed to the principal. The seller's motivation is not a material fact about the property, it is information that would harm the client's bargaining position.
questions.tip: Material facts are about the PROPERTY. Motivation, finances and the lowest price a seller will take are confidential.

questions.q: The fiduciary duties owed to a principal are often remembered as OLD CAR. What does the C stand for?
questions.why: OLD CAR is Obedience, Loyalty, Disclosure, Confidentiality, Accounting, Reasonable care and diligence.
questions.tip: If you remember nothing else about agency, remember OLD CAR. Several exam questions hang off it.

questions.q: An agent represents both buyer and seller in the same transaction without telling either. This is:
choices: Dual agency, legal in every state with a signed form
Undisclosed dual agency, which is illegal
questions.why: Undisclosed dual agency is illegal everywhere. Disclosed dual agency is permitted in some states with informed written consent, and prohibited outright in others.
questions.tip: The exam's trap is the word 'undisclosed'. Read carefully.

questions.q: A broker hired to manage an owner's entire portfolio of rental properties on an ongoing basis is what kind of agent?
questions.why: A general agent handles ongoing business of a continuing nature. A special agent is hired for one specific task, which is what a listing agent usually is.
questions.tip: Special is single task. General is ongoing. Universal can do anything, which is rare and usually a power of attorney.

questions.q: Which action would most likely create an agency relationship by implication?
choices: An agent showing a buyer homes, advising on offer price and negotiating for weeks with no paperwork
A buyer signing a buyer representation agreement
questions.why: Agency can arise from conduct alone. Acting like someone's agent for long enough can create implied agency with all the duties attached, even without a signed agreement.
questions.tip: This is why unrepresented buyers are risky. Behaviour creates duties.

questions.q: An agency relationship terminates in all of these ways EXCEPT:
choices: The property is destroyed by fire
The buyer's agent gets a better offer from another client
questions.why: Agency ends by performance, expiration, mutual agreement, revocation, death or incapacity of either party, destruction of the property, or bankruptcy. Wanting out is not termination.
questions.tip: A better offer elsewhere is a conflict of interest, not a termination event.

questions.q: A buyer's agent discovers the roof leaks badly. The buyer client asks the agent not to mention it to the lender. The agent should:
choices: Follow the client's instruction, because of the duty of obedience
Refuse, because obedience does not extend to unlawful instructions
questions.why: The duty of obedience covers lawful instructions only. An agent must never follow an instruction that is illegal or fraudulent.
questions.tip: Obedience has a ceiling. Illegal instruction beats fiduciary duty every time on the exam.

questions.q: Under an exclusive right to sell listing, when does the broker earn a commission?
choices: Only if the broker personally finds the buyer
If anyone sells the property during the listing period, including the owner
Only if the seller does not find the buyer
Never, if the owner sells it themselves
questions.why: Exclusive right to sell pays the broker regardless of who procures the buyer. Exclusive agency lets the owner sell it themselves commission free.
questions.tip: Exclusive RIGHT TO SELL is the strongest for the broker. Exclusive AGENCY has the owner loophole.

questions.q: A subagent owes fiduciary duties to:
choices: The buyer they are working with
The listing broker's client, the seller
questions.why: A subagent works through the listing broker and owes duties to the seller, even while physically driving the buyer around. This is why subagency has fallen out of favour.
questions.tip: Working WITH a buyer is not the same as working FOR a buyer.

questions.q: Puffing becomes misrepresentation when:
choices: The statement is an opinion rather than fact
A statement of fact is untrue and relied upon
The agent repeats it more than once
questions.why: 'Best view in town' is opinion and is puffing. 'The roof is three years old' when it is fifteen is a false statement of fact, and if relied upon it is misrepresentation.
questions.tip: Opinion is safe. Verifiable fact is not.

questions.q: Which estate gives the most complete ownership recognised in law?
questions.why: Fee simple absolute is ownership of indefinite duration with no conditions attached. Defeasible fee can be lost if a condition is broken.
questions.tip: Absolute means no strings. Defeasible means 'defeatable'.

questions.q: Two people own property with right of survivorship, equal shares, acquired at the same time on the same deed. This is:
questions.why: Joint tenancy requires the four unities: time, title, interest and possession, and carries right of survivorship. Tenancy in common has none of those requirements and no survivorship.
questions.tip: Four unities: T-TIP. Time, Title, Interest, Possession.

questions.q: A owns property in severalty. This means:
choices: One person or entity owns it alone
It is owned by a married couple
questions.why: Severalty means sole ownership, from 'severed' from others. The wording is deliberately counterintuitive and the exam knows it.
questions.tip: Severalty sounds like 'several' and means the opposite. Expect to be tested on exactly that.

questions.q: A life estate measured by the life of someone other than the life tenant is:
questions.why: Pur autre vie is French for 'for another's life'. The estate ends when that named third party dies, not when the life tenant does.
questions.tip: Pur autre vie: the measuring life belongs to someone else.

questions.q: Which is an example of personal property becoming real property?
choices: A tree is cut down for lumber
Bricks are delivered to a site and built into a wall
A tenant removes a trade fixture
questions.why: Annexation converts personal property to real property. Severance is the reverse: cutting a tree turns real property into personal property.
questions.tip: Annexation attaches. Severance separates.

questions.q: The four government powers over private property are remembered as PETE. The E's are:
questions.why: PETE is Police power, Eminent domain, Taxation, Escheat. Escheat is property reverting to the state when someone dies with no heirs and no will.
questions.tip: Police power is the broad one: zoning, building codes and health rules all sit under it.

questions.q: Which best describes an easement appurtenant?
choices: A personal right that ends when the holder dies
A right that runs with the land and benefits an adjoining parcel
A temporary licence to cross land
questions.why: An easement appurtenant involves a dominant tenement, which benefits, and a servient tenement, which is burdened. It transfers with the land automatically.
questions.tip: Appurtenant needs two parcels. In gross needs only one, and is often utility company rights.

questions.q: A neighbour's fence sits two feet inside the property line. This is:
questions.why: An encroachment is an unauthorised physical intrusion onto another's land. It is usually found by survey and can cloud title.
questions.tip: Encroachment is physical and unauthorised. Easement is a right that has been granted or acquired.

questions.q: Which lien generally takes priority over all others, regardless of when it was recorded?
questions.why: Property tax and special assessment liens take first priority almost universally. Other liens generally rank by recording date.
questions.tip: The government gets paid first. That is the rule to carry into the exam.

questions.q: A homeowner's association can enforce which of the following against an owner?
questions.why: CC&Rs are private deed restrictions enforced by the HOA or other owners, typically by injunction. Zoning and codes are government, not HOA.
questions.tip: Private restrictions can be stricter than zoning. Whichever is more restrictive controls.

questions.q: A property use that was legal before a zoning change and is allowed to continue is:
questions.why: A legal nonconforming use is grandfathered in. It often cannot be expanded, rebuilt after major destruction, or resumed after being abandoned.
questions.tip: Grandfathered equals nonconforming use. A variance is permission granted going forward.

questions.q: An owner wants to build a garage three feet from the lot line where the setback requires ten. They should apply for:
questions.why: A variance permits a deviation from a dimensional requirement, usually where strict application would cause unnecessary hardship unique to that parcel.
questions.tip: Variance is for dimensions and hardship. Conditional use is for a use type the zone allows with conditions.

questions.q: Rezoning one small parcel for the benefit of its owner, against the surrounding plan, is:
questions.why: Spot zoning singles out a parcel for treatment inconsistent with the wider plan, and courts often strike it down.
questions.tip: Spot zoning is generally improper. Say so if the exam asks.

questions.q: Under eminent domain, the government must provide:
questions.why: The Fifth Amendment requires just compensation, generally fair market value. The process of taking is condemnation.
questions.tip: Eminent domain is the power. Condemnation is the process. Just compensation is the price.

questions.q: Government action that so restricts a property's use that it destroys its value, without a formal taking, may lead to a claim of:
questions.why: In inverse condemnation the owner sues the government, arguing a taking has effectively occurred and compensation is owed.
questions.tip: Normal condemnation: government sues. Inverse: owner sues.

questions.q: Which appraisal approach is most appropriate for a single family home in a subdivision of similar homes?
questions.why: Sales comparison is the primary approach for residential property, because recent sales of similar homes are the best evidence of value.
questions.tip: Residential: sales comparison. Income property: income. Unique or brand new: cost.

questions.q: Which approach would an appraiser rely on most for a brand new church with no comparable sales?
questions.why: The cost approach suits special purpose and new construction, where there is no sales or income data. It is land value plus replacement cost, less depreciation.
questions.tip: No comps and no income leaves you with cost.

questions.q: A property produces net operating income of $48,000 and comparable properties sell at an 8 percent capitalisation rate. Its indicated value is:
questions.why: Value equals NOI divided by cap rate. 48,000 divided by 0.08 is 600,000.
questions.tip: IRV: Income equals Rate times Value. Cover the one you want with your thumb.

questions.q: Which is an example of external, sometimes called economic, obsolescence?
choices: A new landfill opening next door
questions.why: External obsolescence comes from outside the property line and is generally incurable, because the owner cannot fix it.
questions.tip: Physical is wear. Functional is bad design. External is the neighbourhood, and it is the one you cannot cure.

questions.q: A four bedroom house with one bathroom suffers from:
questions.why: Functional obsolescence is a defect in the design or layout of the improvement itself, such as a poor bed to bath ratio.
questions.tip: If a better architect could have prevented it, it is functional.

questions.q: The principle that a property's value tends to be set by the cost of acquiring an equally desirable substitute is:
questions.why: Substitution underlies the whole sales comparison approach: a buyer will not pay more than the cost of an equivalent alternative.
questions.tip: Substitution is the single most quoted appraisal principle on the exam.

questions.q: Adding a fourth bedroom costs $40,000 and raises value by $25,000. This illustrates:
questions.why: Contribution says an improvement is worth what it adds to value, not what it costs. Over improving is the classic example.
questions.tip: Cost and value are not the same thing. That distinction is heavily tested.

questions.q: A modest house surrounded by much larger, more expensive homes will tend to be worth more than it would elsewhere. This is:
questions.why: Progression: the value of a lesser property is pulled up by better surrounding properties. Regression is the reverse.
questions.tip: Progression pulls up, regression drags down. The worst house on the best street.

questions.q: A comparable sold for $310,000 and has a garage the subject lacks, worth $15,000. To estimate the subject's value the appraiser:
questions.why: Adjustments are always made to the comparable, never the subject. The comparable is superior, so subtract to bring it down to the subject.
questions.tip: CBS or CIA: Comparable Better, Subtract. Comparable Inferior, Add.

questions.q: A broker's price opinion differs from an appraisal mainly because:
choices: It is not performed by a licensed or certified appraiser
questions.why: A BPO or CMA is a broker's estimate to guide pricing. An appraisal is an independent opinion by a licensed appraiser and is what lenders rely on.
questions.tip: Never call a CMA an appraisal. Several exam questions turn on that.

questions.q: A buyer pays 2 discount points on a $250,000 loan. How much is that?
questions.why: One point is one percent of the LOAN amount, not the purchase price. Two percent of 250,000 is 5,000.
questions.tip: Points are always calculated on the loan. The exam loves offering the purchase price figure as a distractor.

questions.q: A home appraises at $300,000, sells for $310,000, and the buyer borrows $240,000. The loan to value ratio is:
questions.why: LTV uses the LOWER of sale price or appraised value. 240,000 divided by 300,000 is 80 percent.
questions.tip: Lenders lend on the lesser of price or appraisal. That is the whole trick in this question.

questions.q: Private mortgage insurance on a conventional loan is generally required when:
choices: The borrower is a first time buyer
The down payment is less than 20 percent
The loan is a VA loan
questions.why: PMI protects the lender when the borrower has under 20 percent equity. It is a conventional loan feature; FHA has MIP instead.
questions.tip: PMI is conventional. MIP is FHA. VA has a funding fee and no monthly mortgage insurance.

questions.q: Which loan type is available only to eligible veterans and generally allows no down payment?
questions.why: The VA guarantees loans for eligible veterans, service members and some surviving spouses, typically with no down payment and no monthly mortgage insurance.
questions.tip: VA guarantees, FHA insures. Neither of them lends the money.

questions.q: RESPA prohibits which of the following?
choices: Kickbacks and unearned referral fees between settlement service providers
Offering a mortgage to a first time buyer
questions.why: Section 8 of RESPA bars kickbacks, fee splits and unearned fees for referrals of settlement services on federally related mortgage loans.
questions.tip: RESPA is the anti kickback law. If someone is paid for a referral and did no work, RESPA is your answer.

questions.q: Regulation Z, implementing the Truth in Lending Act, primarily requires disclosure of:
choices: The annual percentage rate and total cost of credit
questions.why: TILA and Reg Z require the true cost of borrowing to be disclosed, including the APR, so borrowers can compare offers.
questions.tip: Reg Z equals truth in LENDING. It governs the loan, not the sale.

questions.q: In a mortgage, who is the mortgagor?
questions.why: The borrower gives the mortgage, so the borrower is the mortgagor. The lender receives it and is the mortgagee.
questions.tip: The party ending in -OR gives. The party ending in -EE receives. Same for lessor and lessee, grantor and grantee.

questions.q: A clause allowing a lender to demand the full balance if the property is sold is:
choices: A due on sale, or alienation, clause
questions.why: The due on sale or alienation clause prevents a buyer assuming the loan without lender consent. Acceleration is the broader right to call the balance on default.
questions.tip: Alienation means transfer. Due on sale is the alienation clause.

questions.q: The secondary mortgage market exists to:
choices: Buy existing loans so lenders have funds to lend again
questions.why: Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and Ginnie Mae buy loans from originators, providing liquidity so lenders can keep lending.
questions.tip: Primary market lends to you. Secondary market buys that loan from your lender.

questions.q: In a fully amortised loan, over time the portion of each payment going to interest:
questions.why: Early payments are mostly interest. As the balance falls, interest falls and more of each fixed payment goes to principal.
questions.tip: The payment stays level, the split inside it shifts.

questions.q: The Equal Credit Opportunity Act prohibits discrimination in lending based on all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Age, where the applicant is of legal age
questions.why: ECOA bars discrimination on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, and receipt of public assistance. Creditworthiness itself is a legitimate basis.
questions.tip: ECOA adds marital status, age and public assistance, which Fair Housing does not cover.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the essential elements of a valid contract?
questions.why: The elements are mutual assent, consideration, legally competent parties and lawful objective. Real estate contracts must also be in writing under the statute of frauds. Notarisation is not required for validity.
questions.tip: Notarisation is for recording deeds, not for making a contract valid.

questions.q: A contract signed by a minor is generally:
questions.why: Voidable means one party may disaffirm. The minor can walk away; the adult cannot force performance.
questions.tip: Void equals never existed. Voidable equals one side can escape. Unenforceable equals valid but no court will enforce it.

questions.q: A buyer makes an offer. The seller changes the closing date and signs. This is:
choices: A counteroffer, which rejects the original
questions.why: Any change to terms is a counteroffer. It terminates the original offer, and the original offeror is now free to accept, reject or counter again.
questions.tip: Acceptance must mirror the offer exactly. Change a comma and it is a counteroffer.

questions.q: The statute of frauds requires that contracts for the sale of real estate be:
questions.why: The statute of frauds makes oral real estate sales contracts unenforceable. Writing and signature by the party to be charged are the requirement.
questions.tip: Statute of FRAUDS equals must be in WRITING. Nothing to do with actual fraud.

questions.q: A buyer defaults. The contract says the seller keeps the earnest money as the agreed remedy. This is:
questions.why: Liquidated damages is a sum agreed in advance as the remedy for breach, avoiding a fight about actual loss.
questions.tip: Specific performance forces the sale through. Liquidated damages settles it in money agreed up front.

questions.q: Substituting a new party into an existing contract, releasing the original party, is:
questions.why: Novation replaces a party or obligation and releases the original. Assignment transfers rights but the assignor usually stays liable.
questions.tip: Novation equals NEW and released. Assignment equals passed on but still on the hook.

questions.q: An option contract gives the optionee:
choices: The right, but not the obligation, to buy within a set period
A right of first refusal only
questions.why: The optionee holds a unilateral right to buy at agreed terms. The optionor is bound; the optionee is not.
questions.tip: Options are one sided. Only the seller is committed.

questions.q: A financing contingency in a purchase contract protects:
choices: The seller, by guaranteeing the sale
The buyer, by allowing withdrawal if a loan cannot be obtained
questions.why: It lets the buyer exit and recover earnest money if financing on stated terms is unavailable within the deadline.
questions.tip: Contingencies are exit doors. Ask who is allowed to walk through it.

questions.q: Once a valid purchase contract is signed, the buyer holds what interest in the property?
questions.why: Equitable title passes on contract; legal title passes at closing with the deed. This is the doctrine of equitable conversion.
questions.tip: Equitable title at contract, legal title at closing.

questions.q: Which deed offers the grantee the greatest protection?
questions.why: A general warranty deed warrants title against all defects for the entire history of the property, not just the grantor's period of ownership.
questions.tip: General warranty is the most protection. Quitclaim is the least, and warrants nothing at all.

questions.q: A quitclaim deed is most commonly used to:
choices: Sell a home to a stranger
Clear a cloud on title, such as a possible former spouse's interest
questions.why: A quitclaim conveys whatever interest the grantor has, if any, with no warranties. That makes it ideal for releasing a questionable claim.
questions.tip: Quitclaim equals 'whatever I have, you can have'. It might be nothing.

questions.q: For a deed to be valid, which is required?
questions.why: A deed must be in writing, name the parties, contain a legal description and words of conveyance, and be signed by the grantor, then delivered and accepted. Recording is for notice, not validity.
questions.tip: Recording protects you against third parties. It does not make the deed valid.

questions.q: Recording a deed provides:
questions.why: Recording gives constructive notice: the world is deemed to know, whether it looked or not. Actual notice is what someone genuinely knows.
questions.tip: Constructive equals should have known. Actual equals did know.

questions.q: Acquiring title by occupying land openly, notoriously, continuously and hostilely for the statutory period is:
questions.why: The elements are usually open, notorious, continuous, hostile and exclusive possession for a statutory period. The period varies by state.
questions.tip: The statutory period is state specific. The elements are not.

questions.q: A lender's title insurance policy protects:
choices: The lender, up to the loan amount
questions.why: A lender's policy covers only the lender's interest and shrinks as the loan is paid down. A buyer who wants protection needs an owner's policy.
questions.tip: The lender's policy protects the lender. Buyers who assume otherwise are a common exam scenario.

questions.q: When a person dies without a valid will, they are said to have died:
questions.why: Intestate means no valid will, so property passes by the state's laws of descent. Testate means there is a will.
questions.tip: TEST-ate: they took the test and left a will. IN-testate: they did not.

questions.q: Marketable title means title that is:
choices: Free from reasonable doubt and defects a buyer should not have to accept
Held in fee simple absolute only
questions.why: Marketable title is reasonably free from defect and litigation risk. It does not mean perfect, and it does not require insurance.
questions.tip: Marketable is a legal standard, not an insurance product.

questions.q: How many protected classes does the federal Fair Housing Act cover?
questions.why: Race, color, religion, national origin, sex, familial status and disability. Sex, national origin and religion came with the 1968 Act and its amendments; familial status and disability were added in 1988.
questions.tip: Seven federally. Many states and cities add more, such as source of income or age. Check your state section.

questions.q: An agent tells a buyer 'you would be happier in a neighbourhood with more families like yours'. This is:
questions.why: Steering is directing people toward or away from areas based on a protected class. It is illegal regardless of intent or how helpful it feels.
questions.tip: Steering equals directing people. Blockbusting equals scaring people into selling. Redlining equals refusing to lend in an area.

questions.q: Telling homeowners that property values will fall because a minority group is moving in, to induce them to sell, is:
questions.why: Blockbusting, sometimes called panic selling, is inducing sales by exploiting prejudice about who is moving in. It is a serious Fair Housing violation.
questions.tip: Blockbusting is about panic. Someone is being frightened into selling.

questions.q: Under the federal lead based paint rule, a seller of a home built before 1978 must:
choices: Remove all lead paint before sale
Provide the pamphlet, disclose known hazards, and allow a 10 day inspection period
questions.why: The Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act requires disclosure of known hazards, the EPA pamphlet, and a 10 day opportunity to test, which the buyer may waive.
questions.tip: 1978 is the year, and 10 days is the period. Both are commonly tested.

questions.q: Two competing brokerages agree to both charge a 6 percent commission. This is:
choices: Price fixing, a violation of antitrust law
questions.why: Price fixing between competitors is a per se violation of the Sherman Antitrust Act. Commissions are always negotiable between broker and client.
questions.tip: Antitrust: price fixing, market allocation, group boycotts and tying. Never discuss rates with a competitor.

questions.q: Two brokerages agree to divide a city, with one taking the north and one the south. This is:
questions.why: Allocating markets or customers between competitors is an antitrust violation, even where no prices are discussed.
questions.tip: Any agreement with a competitor that reduces competition is suspect.

questions.q: A material fact that must generally be disclosed to a buyer is:
questions.why: Material facts are physical or legal conditions affecting value or desirability. Latent defects known to the seller or agent must be disclosed.
questions.tip: Property condition equals disclose. Personal information about the seller equals confidential.

questions.q: Commingling means:
choices: Mixing client funds with the broker's own money
Sharing a commission with another broker
questions.why: Commingling is mixing trust funds with business or personal funds. Conversion, which is worse, is actually using them. Both risk licence revocation.
questions.tip: Commingling is mixing. Conversion is spending. Neither is survivable for a licence.

questions.q: An advertisement that shows only the monthly payment for a property triggers additional disclosure under:
questions.why: Under Reg Z, stating a trigger term such as the payment amount, down payment or term requires full disclosure of other credit terms including the APR.
questions.tip: Say a number about the financing and you owe the whole picture.

questions.q: A licensee is asked by a buyer whether a neighbourhood is 'safe' and has 'good schools'. The best response is:
choices: Decline to characterise it, and point to objective public sources the buyer can review
Say it is the best area in town
Refuse to work with the buyer
questions.why: Characterising neighbourhoods risks steering, even when well meant. Directing the buyer to public crime statistics and school data lets them decide.
questions.tip: Give sources, not conclusions. This exact scenario appears constantly.

questions.q: The Americans with Disabilities Act primarily requires which of the following in real estate?
choices: That all homes be wheelchair accessible
That places of public accommodation remove barriers where readily achievable
That landlords pay for all tenant modifications
questions.why: The ADA covers commercial facilities and public accommodations. Fair Housing, separately, requires landlords to allow reasonable modifications, usually at the tenant's expense, and make reasonable accommodations.
questions.tip: ADA is commercial and public. Fair Housing is residential.

questions.q: A lease with a definite start and end date, ending automatically with no notice, is:
questions.why: An estate for years has a fixed term and terminates on the end date without notice, whether that term is one week or ninety nine years.
questions.tip: 'For years' does not mean years. It means a definite term.

questions.q: A tenant stays after the lease expires, without the landlord's permission. This is:
questions.why: A holdover tenant without consent has an estate at sufferance. If the landlord accepts rent, it can convert to a periodic tenancy.
questions.tip: Sufferance is the lowest estate: possession without right but without force.

questions.q: In a triple net lease, the tenant typically pays rent plus:
questions.why: Net leases shift expenses to the tenant. Triple net covers taxes, insurance and maintenance on top of base rent.
questions.tip: Gross lease: landlord pays expenses. Net lease: tenant does. Percentage lease: rent varies with sales, common in retail.

questions.q: A tenant transfers the entire remaining lease term to another party. This is:
questions.why: Transferring the whole remaining interest is an assignment. Keeping any reversionary interest, even a day, makes it a sublease.
questions.tip: Whole remaining term equals assignment. Anything less equals sublease.

questions.q: A landlord shuts off heat and water to force a tenant out. The tenant may claim:
questions.why: Constructive eviction occurs when a landlord's act or neglect makes the premises unusable, allowing the tenant to leave and stop paying.
questions.tip: Actual eviction is the sheriff. Constructive is the landlord making it unliveable.

questions.q: A home sells for $325,000 with a 6 percent commission split evenly between listing and selling brokerages. What does the listing brokerage receive?
questions.why: Total commission is 325,000 times 0.06, which is 19,500. Split evenly gives each brokerage 9,750.
questions.tip: Read carefully whether the question wants total, brokerage share, or the individual agent's share after their own split.

questions.q: How many square feet are in an acre?
questions.why: One acre is 43,560 square feet. A section is 640 acres and one square mile. A township is 36 sections.
questions.tip: 43,560 is the single most useful number to memorise. 5,280 is feet in a mile.

questions.q: A lot measures 150 feet by 290.4 feet. Approximately how many acres is it?
questions.why: 150 times 290.4 is 43,560 square feet, which is exactly one acre.
questions.tip: Multiply the sides, then divide by 43,560.

questions.q: A seller wants $200,000 net after paying a 6 percent commission. What must the property sell for?
questions.why: Net divided by (100 percent minus the rate). 200,000 divided by 0.94 is 212,765.96. Multiplying by 1.06 is the classic wrong answer.
questions.tip: Net to seller: divide, never multiply. 212,000 is the trap.

questions.q: Annual property taxes are $3,650, paid in arrears. Closing is on day 100 of a 365 day year. Using a 365 day proration, what does the seller owe the buyer?
questions.why: Daily rate is 3,650 divided by 365, which is 10 dollars. The seller owned for 100 days, so 100 times 10 is 1,000 owed to the buyer, who will pay the full bill.
questions.tip: Taxes in arrears: the seller credits the buyer for the time the seller owned.

questions.q: A property generates $60,000 in gross annual rent and sells for $480,000. What is the gross rent multiplier, using annual rent?
questions.why: GRM is price divided by rent. 480,000 divided by 60,000 is 8.
questions.tip: Check whether the question uses monthly or annual rent. Residential GRM is often monthly, which changes the answer entirely.

questions.q: A buyer borrows $180,000 at 5 percent interest. What is the first month's interest portion?
questions.why: Annual interest is 180,000 times 0.05, which is 9,000. Divided by 12 months gives 750.
questions.tip: Annual first, then divide by twelve. Do not divide the rate by twelve and then panic.

questions.q: A property's potential gross income is $100,000, vacancy is 5 percent, and operating expenses are $30,000. What is the net operating income?
questions.why: Effective gross income is 100,000 less 5,000 vacancy, which is 95,000. Subtract 30,000 expenses for an NOI of 65,000.
questions.tip: NOI never subtracts debt service or income tax. That trips people constantly.

questions.q: An investor buys for $250,000 and sells for $300,000. What is the percentage of profit?
questions.why: Profit of 50,000 divided by the original cost of 250,000 is 20 percent. Percentage change always uses the starting figure as the base.
questions.tip: Divide by what you started with, not what you ended with.

questions.q: A house is assessed at $180,000 and the tax rate is 25 mills. What is the annual tax?
questions.why: A mill is one thousandth of a dollar, so 25 mills is 0.025. 180,000 times 0.025 is 4,500.
questions.tip: Mills: divide by 1,000. 25 mills equals 0.025, or 2.5 percent.
